questions.question: Which ancient Indian philosopher postulated that matter can be divided into extremely small, indivisible particles called 'Parmanu' around 500 BC?
questions.explanation: Around 500 BC, the Indian philosopher Maharishi Kanad postulated the atomic theory, suggesting that matter (padarth) divided into smaller particles would eventually reach a limit where it cannot be divided further, naming these particles 'Parmanu'.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek philosopher named the ultimate, indivisible particles of matter 'atoms' (derived from 'atomos')?
questions.explanation: Building on similar philosophical ideas, the Greek philosopher Democritus named these indivisible building blocks of matter 'atoms' (from the Greek word 'atomos', meaning indivisible).

questions.question: Which two ancient Greek philosophers are credited with suggesting that matter can be divided until an ultimate, indivisible particle called an 'atom' is reached?
questions.explanation: Democritus and his mentor Leucippus were the ancient Greek philosophers who proposed that matter is made up of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms (atomos).

questions.question: Which scientist is credited with formulating the Law of Constant Proportions?
questions.explanation: Joseph Proust formulated the Law of Constant Proportions, stating that a chemical compound always contains exactly the same elements combined in the same proportions by mass.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs the scientist with the law they formulated?
options: Antoine Lavoisier - Law of Constant Proportions
Joseph Proust - Law of Conservation of Mass
Antoine Lavoisier - Law of Conservation of Mass
Joseph Proust - Law of Multiple Proportions
questions.explanation: Antoine Lavoisier formulated the Law of Conservation of Mass, whereas Joseph Proust formulated the Law of Constant Proportions.

questions.question: Which of the following two laws form the foundational Laws of Chemical Combination discussed in early chemistry?
options: Law of Conservation of Mass and Law of Constant Proportions
Law of Definite Energy and Law of Multiple Proportions
Law of Conservation of Energy and Law of Gravitation
questions.explanation: The two principal laws of chemical combination that laid the groundwork for atomic theory are the Law of Conservation of Mass (Lavoisier) and the Law of Constant Proportions (Proust).

questions.question: Which of the following best illustrates the Law of Constant Proportions for a sample of pure water (H2O)?
options: The mass ratio of hydrogen to oxygen in water changes depending on whether it is river water or rainwater
Hydrogen and oxygen are always combined in a fixed mass ratio of 1:8 by mass, regardless of the water's source
Water can have any random proportion of hydrogen and oxygen depending on how it was heated
The elements in water combine in a fixed volume ratio of 1:1 regardless of their masses
questions.explanation: According to the Law of Constant Proportions, a chemical compound like water always contains the same elements in the same fixed proportion by mass (1 part hydrogen to 8 parts oxygen), no matter where the sample is obtained.

questions.question: According to the Law of Constant Proportions, what is the fixed mass ratio of nitrogen to hydrogen in a pure sample of ammonia (NH3)?
questions.explanation: In ammonia (NH3), one nitrogen atom (mass 14 u) combines with three hydrogen atoms (mass 3 × 1 = 3 u), giving a fixed mass ratio of nitrogen to hydrogen of 14:3.

questions.question: How did Joseph Proust formally state the Law of Definite Proportions?
options: Mass can neither be created nor destroyed during a physical change.
In a chemical substance, the elements are always present in definite proportions by mass.
Gases combine in simple whole-number volume ratios under similar conditions of temperature and pressure.
Energy is directly proportional to mass in any isolated chemical system.
questions.explanation: Joseph Proust stated that in a chemical substance, the elements are always present in definite proportions by mass, meaning the composition of a pure compound is independent of its source or method of preparation.

questions.question: Whose atomic theory provided the theoretical foundation and explanation for the Law of Conservation of Mass and the Law of Constant Proportions?
questions.explanation: John Dalton's atomic theory (1808) used the concept of indestructible and indivisible atoms to successfully explain both the Law of Conservation of Mass and the Law of Constant Proportions.

questions.question: In which year was John Dalton, the scientist who proposed the modern atomic theory, born?
questions.explanation: John Dalton was born on September 6, 1766, in England, and later published his groundbreaking atomic theory in 1808.

questions.question: In which place was John Dalton born?
questions.explanation: John Dalton was born on September 6, 1766, in Eaglesfield, Cumberland, England.

questions.question: At what age did John Dalton begin his career as a teacher?
questions.explanation: John Dalton showed an early aptitude for learning and began teaching younger students at his local village school at the young age of 12.

questions.question: At what age did John Dalton become a school principal/head of a school in Kendal?
questions.explanation: Having started teaching very early in life, John Dalton took on the role of running a school in Kendal alongside his brother when he reached the age of 19.

questions.question: At which institution did John Dalton serve as a teacher of mathematics and natural philosophy starting in 1793?
questions.explanation: John Dalton moved to Manchester in 1793 to teach mathematics and natural philosophy (encompassing physics and chemistry) at New College.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the core postulates of John Dalton's atomic theory?
options: Atoms of different elements have different masses and chemical properties.
Compounds are formed when atoms combine in fixed ratios of small whole numbers.
Atoms can be broken down further into subatomic particles like protons, neutrons, and electrons during a chemical reaction.
Atoms are indivisible particles that cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.
questions.explanation: Dalton's original atomic theory regarded atoms as completely indivisible and indestructible. The discovery of subatomic particles (protons, neutrons, and electrons) later proved that atoms can indeed be subdivided, which was a limitation of Dalton's original theory.

questions.question: What is the chemical formula of acetic acid, which gives vinegar its characteristic sour taste and pungent smell?
questions.explanation: Acetic acid has the chemical formula CH3COOH (ethanoic acid) and is the primary active ingredient in vinegar besides water.

questions.question: What is the common trivial name for ethanoic acid (CH3COOH)?
questions.explanation: Ethanoic acid is the IUPAC name, while its widely used common name is acetic acid, which forms the basis of household vinegar.

questions.question: What is the correct chemical formula for sodium acetate?
questions.explanation: Sodium acetate is formed by replacing the hydrogen atom in the carboxyl group of acetic acid (CH3COOH) with a sodium ion, resulting in the chemical formula CH3COONa.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly represents the chemical formula and charge of the acetate ion?
questions.explanation: The acetate ion has the chemical formula CH3COO- with a single negative charge, formed when acetic acid loses its acidic proton (H+).

questions.question: Which of the following best defines an atom in the context of chemistry?
options: A macroscopic substance formed by combining two or more different molecules.
The smallest particle of an element that takes part in a chemical reaction and retains the element's properties.
A subatomic particle that exists independently without any association with elements.
A pure compound created by the physical mixing of different types of matter.
questions.explanation: An atom is defined as the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction while still retaining the chemical properties of that element.

questions.question: What is the approximate atomic radius of a hydrogen atom, which is the smallest known atom?
questions.explanation: Atoms are extremely tiny, with atomic radii typically on the order of 10^-9 meters (or 1 nanometers), with hydrogen being the smallest.

questions.question: How many nanometers are there in 1 meter?
questions.explanation: Since 1 meter equals 10^9 nanometers (one billion nanometers), 1 m = 1,000,000,000 nm.

questions.question: Which of the following statements best defines a chemical element?
options: A heterogeneous mixture of various types of atoms physically combined together.
A compound formed by the chemical combination of two or more different elements.
A complex substance that can easily be split into simpler components using basic physical methods.
A pure substance composed of only one kind of atom that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means.
questions.explanation: An element is defined as a pure form of matter consisting of only one type of atom, which cannot be broken down into simpler chemical substances by ordinary chemical reactions.

questions.question: According to the historical development in chemistry, who was the first scientist to use specific symbols to represent elements and their atoms?
questions.explanation: John Dalton was the first scientist to use specific symbols (such as circles with unique patterns or letters inside) to represent atoms of different elements.

questions.question: Which prominent chemist proposed the modern system of using the first letter or the first two letters of an element's English or Latin name as its symbol?
questions.explanation: Jöns Jacob Berzelius introduced the letter-based system of chemical symbols in 1813, using either the first letter or the first two letters of an element's name.

questions.question: Which metal got its name from the island of Cyprus, where it was extensively mined in ancient times?
questions.explanation: Copper derives its name from the island of Cyprus, reflecting how early elements were often named after their geographic place of origin or discovery.

questions.question: The name of which precious metal originates from an English word meaning 'yellow'?
questions.explanation: The word 'gold' comes from an old English root meaning 'yellow', reflecting how early elements were often named based on their physical appearance or color.

questions.question: Which international scientific organization is officially responsible for approving names and symbols for chemical elements?
options: IUPAC (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry)
questions.explanation: IUPAC (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry) is the global authority that regulates and approves the official names, symbols, and terminology of chemical elements.

questions.question: Which isotope is universally accepted as the standard reference for measuring atomic masses in chemistry today in 1961?
questions.explanation: The carbon-12 (12C) isotope is used as the standard reference atom, where 1 atomic mass unit (u) is defined as 1/12th the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

questions.question: According to modern chemical standards, exactly what fraction of a carbon-12 atom's mass defines 1 atomic mass unit (1 u)?
questions.explanation: 1 atomic mass unit (u) is precisely defined as 1/12th of the mass of an unbound atom of carbon-12 at rest in its ground state.

questions.question: What is Atomic number?
options: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom
The number of neutrons in the nucleus of an atom
The number of electrons in the nucleus of an atom
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom
questions.explanation: The atomic number is defined as the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, which determines the identity of the element.

questions.question: What is Mass number?
options: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom
The number of neutrons in the nucleus of an atom
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom
The total number of electrons in the atom
questions.explanation: The mass number is defined as the total number of protons and neutrons present in the nucleus of an atom.

questions.question: What are molecules?
options: A single atom of an element
A group of two or more atoms chemically bonded together, capable of existing independently and retaining the chemical properties of the substance.
An ion with a net charge
questions.explanation: A molecule is defined as a group of two or more atoms chemically bonded together.

questions.question: What is the difference between an atom and a molecule?
options: An atom is a single particle of an element, while a molecule is a group of two or more atoms chemically bonded together.
An atom is a group of two or more atoms chemically bonded together, while a molecule is a single particle of an element.
An atom can exist independently, while a molecule cannot.
There is no difference; they are the same.
questions.explanation: An atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical properties, while a molecule consists of two or more atoms bonded together, which can be of the same or different elements.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a diatomic molecule?
questions.explanation: A diatomic molecule consists of two atoms. Oxygen (O2) is an example of a diatomic molecule, as it is composed of two oxygen atoms bonded together.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct definition of atomicity?
options: The number of atoms constituting a single molecule.
The total mass of all atoms present in a molecule.
The number of protons and neutrons in an atom's nucleus.
The fixed ratio by mass in which elements combine to form a compound.
questions.explanation: Atomicity simply refers to how many atoms make up one molecule of an element or compound. For example, O2 has an atomicity of 2.

questions.question: Which of the following elements is classified as monoatomic?
questions.explanation: Helium is a noble gas and exists as single, unbonded atoms, making it monoatomic.

questions.question: To include all 6 noble gases in a 4-option question, they are grouped in pairs. Which of the following options does NOT consist entirely of noble gases?
questions.explanation: Options A, B, and C successfully group all 6 noble gases in pairs. Option D contains Nitrogen and Oxygen, which are diatomic gases.

questions.question: What is the fixed ratio by mass of carbon to oxygen in a carbon dioxide (CO2) molecule?
questions.explanation: Carbon has a total mass of 12 u and Oxygen has a total mass of 32 u in CO2. The ratio 12 : 32 simplifies to 3 : 8.

questions.question: What is the ratio by number of atoms for a water molecule (H2O)?
questions.explanation: A water molecule (H2O) contains 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom, giving a ratio by number of atoms of 2 : 1.

questions.question: What is the fixed ratio by mass of hydrogen to oxygen in a water molecule (H2O)?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen has a total mass of 2 u and Oxygen has a mass of 16 u in H2O. The ratio 2 : 16 simplifies to 1 : 8.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines an ion?
options: An atom with an equal number of protons and electrons.
A neutral molecule composed of two or more identical atoms.
A charged atom or group of atoms carrying a net positive or negative charge.
An unstable subatomic particle found only inside the nucleus.
questions.explanation: An ion is an atom or group of atoms that has acquired an electric charge by gaining or losing electrons.

questions.question: What is an anion?
options: A positively charged ion formed by losing electrons.
A negatively charged ion formed by gaining electrons.
A neutral atom with equal numbers of protons and electrons.
A molecule with no net electrical charge.
questions.explanation: An anion is a negatively charged ion created when an atom or group of atoms gains one or more electrons.

questions.question: What is a cation?
options: A negatively charged ion formed by gaining electrons.
A neutral atom with no electrons.
A molecule formed by sharing electrons.
A positively charged ion formed by losing electrons.
questions.explanation: A cation is a positively charged ion created when an atom or group of atoms loses one or more electrons.

questions.question: Is the chloride ion (Cl-) a cation or an anion?
questions.explanation: Cl- carries a negative sign, indicating it is a negatively charged ion, which is defined as an anion.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines the valency of an element?
options: The total number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The combining capacity of an atom of an element.
The total mass of all electrons in an atom.
The total number of neutrons and protons combined.
questions.explanation: Valency refers to the combining capacity of an atom, representing how many electrons it uses to bond with other atoms.

questions.question: Which of the following represents a binary compound?
questions.explanation: Water (H2O) is a binary compound because it consists of exactly two different elements (Hydrogen and Oxygen).

questions.question: What is the molecular mass of water (H2O), given that the atomic mass of H is 1u and O is 16u?
questions.explanation: Molecular mass is calculated by adding the atomic masses of all atoms: (2 x 1 u for hydrogen) + (1 x 16 u for oxygen) = 18 u.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines molecular mass?
options: The mass of a single proton in an atom's nucleus.
The sum of the atomic masses of all atoms present in a molecule.
The fixed ratio by mass in which elements combine.
The total number of electrons surrounding a nucleus.
questions.explanation: Molecular mass is calculated by adding up the individual atomic masses of every atom that makes up a single molecule.

questions.question: What is the main difference between molecular mass and formula unit mass?
options: Formula unit mass uses addition, while molecular mass uses multiplication.
They are calculated differently using completely different atomic masses.
Molecular mass is for covalent molecules, while formula unit mass is for ionic compounds.
Formula unit mass only applies to gases.
questions.explanation: The math is identical for both, but we use molecular mass for discrete molecules and formula unit mass for ionic compounds that exist in giant crystal structures.

questions.question: What is the charge of a sodium ion when it forms a cation?
questions.explanation: Sodium loses its single valence electron to achieve stability, giving it a net charge of +1 (Na+).

questions.question: What is the charge of a potassium ion when it forms a cation?
questions.explanation: Potassium is in Group 1 and loses its single valence electron, leaving it with a net positive charge of +1 (K+).

questions.question: What is the common charge of a silver ion in its compounds?
questions.explanation: Silver most commonly loses one electron to form a stable +1 ion (Ag+).

questions.question: What is the charge of a copper(I) (cuprous) ion?
questions.explanation: The Roman numeral (I) in copper(I) indicates that the ion has a positive charge of +1.

questions.question: What is the common charge of a magnesium ion?
questions.explanation: Magnesium is in Group 2 and loses its 2 valence electrons, resulting in a net positive charge of +2 (Mg2+).

questions.question: What is the common charge of a calcium ion in chemical compounds?
questions.explanation: Calcium is a Group 2 element that loses its 2 valence electrons, resulting in a +2 charge (Ca2+).

questions.question: What is the common charge of a zinc ion in chemical compounds?
questions.explanation: Zinc consistently loses its two outermost electrons to form a stable +2 ion (Zn2+).

questions.question: What is the charge of an iron(II) (ferrous) ion?
questions.explanation: The Roman numeral (II) in iron(II) indicates that the metal ion has a positive charge of +2.

questions.question: What is the charge of a copper(II) (cupric) ion?
questions.explanation: The Roman numeral (II) in copper(II) indicates a positive charge of +2.

questions.question: What is the common charge of an aluminium ion in chemical compounds?
questions.explanation: Aluminium is in Group 13 and loses its 3 valence electrons, resulting in a net positive charge of +3 (Al3+).

questions.question: What is the charge of an iron(III) (ferric) ion?
questions.explanation: The Roman numeral (III) in iron(III) indicates that the metal ion has a positive charge of +3.

questions.question: What is the most common positive ionic charge or valency associated with hydrogen in standard acids?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen most commonly exhibits a valency of 1 and forms a +1 charge (H+) in acids.

questions.question: What is the charge of a hydride ion when hydrogen combines with active metals?
questions.explanation: When hydrogen gains an electron to form a hydride ion in metal hydrides, it acquires a -1 charge.

questions.question: What is the common charge of a chloride ion when chlorine forms an ionic compound?
questions.explanation: Chlorine is a halogen that gains 1 electron to complete its outer shell, resulting in a -1 charge (Cl-).

questions.question: What is the common charge of a bromide ion when bromine forms an ionic compound?
questions.explanation: Bromine gains 1 electron to complete its outer shell, resulting in a -1 charge (Br-).

questions.question: What is the common charge of an iodide ion when iodine forms an ionic compound?
questions.explanation: Iodine gains 1 electron to complete its outer shell, resulting in a -1 charge (I-).

questions.question: What is the common charge of an oxide ion when oxygen forms an ionic compound?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is in Group 16 and gains 2 electrons to complete its outer shell, resulting in a -2 charge (O2-).

questions.question: What is the common charge of a sulphide ion when sulfur forms an ionic compound?
questions.explanation: Sulfur gains 2 electrons to complete its outer shell, resulting in a -2 charge (S2-).

questions.question: What is the common charge of a nitride ion when nitrogen forms an ionic compound with metals?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is in Group 15 and gains 3 electrons to complete its outer shell, resulting in a -3 charge (N3-).

questions.question: What is the common charge of an ammonium polyatomic ion?
questions.explanation: The ammonium ion (NH4+) carries a net positive charge of +1.

questions.question: What is the charge of the hydroxide polyatomic ion?
questions.explanation: The hydroxide ion carries a net charge of -1.

questions.question: What is the charge of the nitrate polyatomic ion?
questions.explanation: The nitrate ion consists of one nitrogen and three oxygen atoms with a net -1 charge, written as NO3-.

questions.question: What is the charge of the hydrogen carbonate (bicarbonate) polyatomic ion?
questions.explanation: The hydrogen carbonate ion carries a net charge of -1.

questions.question: What is the charge of the carbonate polyatomic ion?
questions.explanation: The carbonate ion carries a net charge of -2.

questions.question: What is the charge of the sulphite (sulfite) polyatomic ion?
questions.explanation: The sulphite ion carries a net charge of -2.

questions.question: What is the charge of the sulphate (sulfate) polyatomic ion?
questions.explanation: The sulphate ion carries a net charge of -2.

questions.question: What is the charge of the phosphate polyatomic ion?
questions.explanation: The phosphate ion carries a net charge of -3.
